articles.title: Xbox Design Chief Reveals the Surprising Ikea Item That Shaped Every Console
articles.summary: Xbox design chief Carl Ledbetter reveals how an Ikea bookcase inspired the console’s design, as Xbox and Ikea launch the new YXSTABY furniture line.
articles.body:
Gamescom kicks off today in Cologne, Germany, and among the many big game debuts, hands-on demos, and major announcements is a new kind of reveal: Xbox is partnering with Ikea to sell an exclusive set of Xbox-inspired furniture and accessories that you can buy starting this fall. But, according to Xbox, the new collection goes far beyond the typical gamer chair and desk setup.

Carl Ledbetter, head of design at Xbox, has been at Microsoft for more than 30 years (dating back to the days of the IntelliMouse) and is responsible for designing consoles like the Xbox One and Xbox Series X|S. Ledbetter led the charge with the Ikea collaboration and says the partnership isn’t as unusual as you might suspect . I spoke to Ledbetter exclusively at gamescom ahead of the reveal of YXSTABY (get it?) a “nine-piece collection designed for gaming at home,” and found out that Xbox’s ties to Ikea go back further than you might expect.

An iconic Ikea bookcase influenced the Xbox shape

“The piece of furniture that we use as our de facto test for any console design is the Billy bookcase from Ikea,” Ledbetter says. “So believe it or not, it's a natural fit. I’ve spent all my time [at Xbox] looking at input, controllers, the console, how things fit into the home. [That] matters when you design a console, [the] horizontal and vertical position. [So] this goes back years. The philosophy that we share for designing products at Xbox and at Ikea are nearly identical. So it was like a love connection.”

XBOX YXSTABY Full Lineup Revealed - Exclusive

IGN can exclusively reveal a look at the entire collection, which features nine pieces, including chairs with console pockets, thumbstick-shaped stools, a D-Pad inspired platter to hold your controller, X-shaped pillows, and more. Ledbetter says that planning a series of pieces intended to be picked up, sat on, leaned against, and otherwise interacted with came with a surprising challenge.

“Xbox and Ikea, they both have scale,” Ledbetter says. “We designed for millions of players around the world. Ikea’s already there. The thing that is different, at least for my team and designing this line, was taking into consideration the flat pack. So Ikea, of course [uses a flat pack] in order to ship these things all around the world. When you buy a console, the most you have to do is plug it in and turn it on. But in this case, you have some assembly required. It was just fascinating to work with them side by side and see how to problem-solve. That was pretty fun.” Ledbetter says that, although bringing a collection of furniture to life is inherently different than building a new console, his overarching design philosophy didn’t change.

“First and foremost, the product's got to work,” Ledbetter says. “It has to solve real problems. Whether it's a controller or a piece of furniture, it's the same thing. The second thing is, for gamers, particularly when they're playing Xbox games at home, it's about immersion. It’s in the game you see on the screen and in the controller you hold in your hand. But if you think about it, it's everything around you. The products you sit on, the things that hold your TV, etc. We started talking about those challenges for players and immediately started coming up together with ideas. We tried to find balance.

“The question that the Ikea designers had for me was, ‘Carl, what are the iconic elements of Xbox?’ Number one is the controller. While we've improved it and changed it over time, it's very recognizable. And so there are elements that people interact with on the controller that they just sort of bubbled up to the top. The D-pad was one. So you see the D-pad platter, the D-pad pillow. And of course the thumbstick was just right there. It's such an interactive and engaging thing. We landed on the thumbstick stool.”

Xbox designer reveals the new YXSTABY furniture collection contains plenty of hidden details

Ledbetter says that for hardcore Xbox fans, there will be plenty of Easter eggs when the YXSTABY collection hits stores this fall.

“If you look at the TV stand or the monitor stand, if you look at the detailing that the designers have put on these products, they’re super clean,” Ledbetter says. “There's nothing extra. The materials are honest and authentic. Those same [XBOX] design qualities are used throughout the entire collection.

“They may not stand out immediately. We call it the second level read, third level read. You start to notice the subtleties of these things. There are some subtle things. If you look at the gaming chair, we used green stitching. It is super, super subtle, but for those who know, they'll know. They'll recognize these little qualities.”

The new Xbox furniture line will have plenty of accessibility features

Ledbetter, who contributed to the design of Xbox’s revolutionary adaptive controller, says designing YXSTABY for all gamers was just as important as throwing in subtle nods to hardcore fans.

“The more people who can use the product, the better,” Ledbetter says. “The gaming chair is designed for two types of gaming postures. The first one is just sitting up. It's the leaning forward posture. [For games like] Gears of War: E-Day, maybe you're getting sweaty and it's intense. And then what happens when you beat the boss? [You go back.] Also, what we found in the prototyping process of the pillow is you can actually take it and rest your arms when you play. It creates a really cool experience.

“[Another] accessible design is the monitor stand. You can put the monitor on it and it's more ergonomic, at eye level. So it gets you in a better posture. And then underneath you can put your mouse, keyboard, and a laptop under there. It can fit an Xbox Series S. And then it has all these configurable stands for your headset, for your cellphone. There's a spot in there to charge your controllers. So we really try to accommodate different people and what their needs are.”

Ledbetter would like to build an Xbox-inspired house

Throughout his long career at Microsoft, Ledbetter has had the chance to design a number of popular, iconic products whose form is immediately recognizable to gamers and non-gamers alike. And while he’s pleased with how the Ikea collaboration has turned out, he says there’s one major Xbox adaptation he’d still like to tackle if given the opportunity.

“The Xbox One X, when it came out, the Scorpio [edition] was the smallest and most powerful console we'd ever made,” Ledbetter says. “But if you look at that, it sort of has this layered design to it. It'd be fun to turn that into a home. [It could be] very inspired by [Frank Lloyd Wright's] Falling Water with little layers. [It makes sense because] the purity of the designs of our consoles are designed to be as expressive or quiet as people want them to be.”

YXSTABY is being unveiled this week at gamescom and will be available in Ikea stores and online this fall.

articles.title: Metro 2039: The First Hands-On Preview
articles.summary: In an age where single-player first-person shooters are slowly going extinct because they only make money for their publisher once while multiplayer live-service shooters vie for our time and attention on a daily basis (and often contain lots of bullsh*t, like microtransactions and/or drawn-out gameplay loops), Metro 2039’s single-player-only craftsmanship and attention to detail after my first few hours with it have me already prepared to call it my favorite first-person shooter in a long time.
articles.body:
Metro 2039, very refreshingly, doesn't hold your hand. It throws you straight into the deep end.

This franchise always was, of course; this is nothing new.

But still, there’s just something about the way 2039 is hitting for me at this exact moment in time that I needed. It is a game that neither offers nor tolerates any bullsh*t, and I love it for that because said bullsh*t surrounds us in the real world. Metro does not hold your hand. It regularly keeps your blood pressure somewhere between slightly elevated and spiked, and it makes no apologies for it. Its irradiated world is Hell, and it very convincingly conveys that at all times. And in an age where single-player first-person shooters are slowly going extinct because they only make money for their publisher once while multiplayer live-service shooters vie for our time and attention on a daily basis (and often contain lots of bullsh*t, like microtransactions and/or drawn-out gameplay loops), Metro’s single-player-only craftsmanship and attention to detail after my first few hours with it have me already prepared to call it my favorite first-person shooter in a long time.

If you’ve played Metro before you’ll certainly be right at home, but even if you’re new to this series, it’s easy enough to get up to speed with. In short, everything is lethal, from the mutated monstrosities on the surface to rival survivors who’ve laid claim to the places you need to get through to the very air you breathe. You are almost never, ever “safe” in Metro 2039. The one place you can’t get killed is where my preview build started out in the Sevastopolskaya Metro Station, which is filled with NPCs and shopkeepers. It feels very alive – a stark contrast to the 180 that happens as soon as you grab your backpack and gun and exit the metro and head to the very dead surface.

There, you are completely and utterly alone. Not literally, as there are mutated freaks abound, from giant maneating rats to jumpy beasts that like to keep their distance and fling barbs from their tails at you to oversized mosquitos who like to get right in your face to huge prehistoric-sized crustaceans who emerge from the waters of the sewers. And, as mentioned, there are plenty of other survivors out there too. Except all of them are hostile – or at least, everyone I met outside of the metro during my hands-on time immediately wanted me dead.

I appreciated being thrown straight into the deep end as soon as I reached the surface. Yes, a map on a crude tablet gave me a general idea of where to go towards my next objective, but beyond that I was on my own to figure out the best path – and to survive along the way. I wandered into a drug store – well, the picked-apart remnan ts of one, obviously – and I checked every nook and cranny for crafting items I could use to make medkits, ammo, and most crucially of all, new gas mask filters. Pressing Y on the keyboard lifts your gun up a little higher so you can clearly see your digital wristwatch, which constantly ticks down the minutes and seconds until your current filter will expire.

I found environmental puzzles tucked away in various places, and felt compelled to try and solve them all because the reward would likely be those precious crafting resources that would well and truly keep me alive. Some of these puzzles utilized the Stranger’s UV light, guiding you to follow clues that were scrawled on walls and floors such that they could only be seen under the purple hue. In my experience, these challenges may have been optional, but they were worth pursuing every single time. Again, it can’t be said enough: Metro 2039 does not mess around. It does not waste your time. There doesn’t seem to be any filler content here. Everything seems to be meticulously considered and implemented.

The weapons are something of a puzzle unto themselves. They can all be modified and customized, from their scopes to their hilts to their muzzles and more. At one point fairly early on, I found a double-barrelled sho tgun that I decided to swap out for the single-barrel version I had on me, and it became my go-to gun in the close-quarters “dungeons” I spent much of the latter half of my demo traipsing through. I even found a laser sight to attach to it, which is almost comically pointless on a close-quarters death-dealer like this, but I didn’t have anything better to stick on there, so I figured, “What the heck.”

Oh, and as you may very well have guessed by now, ammo is scarce . You can find and craft different types – everything from rudimentary metal balls to incendiary rounds to armor-piercing machinegun rounds – and you’ll certainly need to. I survived a miniboss fight with a nine-foot-tall mutant and his feral accomplices with so few rounds left on me that I prayed there was nothing else waiting for me for the next little while, because the fight took place in knee-deep sewer water, which meant that I had nowhere I could set my backpack down in order to craft more. (Fortunately, Metro’s game designers took pity on me, and I was indeed given a short reprieve.)

But you also have throwables that help tilt the scales slightly back in your favor. I was quite fond of the knives, as not only can they enable you to stealthily take out regular human enemies without alerting anyone else, but as you’d expect in a game with such stringent resource management, you can retrieve your blades from the corpses of your targets (or the ground if you happen to miss a throw). But as the caliber of foe ramped up as I progressed, the Molotov cocktails started to get a lot more useful.

Adding to the list of things I love about Metro 2039 so far is its gameplay variety. I was never doing the same thing for very long during my few hours with it, and I applaud it for that. As I mentioned, I started with a rare moment of safety in the metro station before moving topside and having plenty of room to roam while contending with the mutated bestiary I talked about earlier. And as I progressed, I was kept on my toes with a number of different gameplay scenarios.

At one point, I was conveniently left a scoped rifle on the decaying second-story balcony of a building adjacent to a nest of Novoreich members – they’re the bad-guy faction here, under the direction of Fuhrer Hunter, who was only teased in my demo, so I can’t really determine much about the quality of him as a foe, besides the fact that he is very obviously a post-apocalyptic Hitler and therefore I’ll take great pleasure in gunning him and everyone in his ranks down in the final game. Sadly I don’t have any footage of this to show you.

Anyway, I picked up that scoped rifle and started loudly picking off Novoreich scum – they told on themselves by having bright lights attached to their weapons, making things easier for me. Later, in a completely different scenario, I found myself in an abandoned da ycare, where my electronics got jammed in one particularly creepy room, making my skin crawl despite there being nary a living creature around and motivating me to want to get the heck out of there as quickly as possible.

Thankfully, you do get a break from the constant juggling act of crafting and installing new gas mask filters in Metro’s subterranean “dungeons,” at least. The air is clean enough in these to be able to safely remove your gas mask, and in the several I battled through, all favored close-quarters combat, which made me all-too-happy to bust out that double-barrelled shotgun I’d picked up early on. In one of them, I was able to choke out the only upstairs guard without alerting anyone below, and he was conveniently standing (well, slouching now) next to an open air duct that let me creep down silently and in the shadows to the dark main base below, which was teeming with unfriendly humans. I botched my stealth attempt here trying to thread the needle with a thrown knife at a tough angle, and I got discovered. It then became an old-fashioned shootout, in which I was happy to break out Metro’s lean feature from behind cover to expose as little of my body to the baddies as possible.

This was the story of my hands-on time: combat encounters came in many different forms, shapes, and sizes, and I really appreciated that.

Speaking of appreciation, it will come as no surprise to anyone that’s played a Metro game before that 2039 is, visually speaking, gorgeous. It’s bleak and horrifying, of course, but it’s rendered beautifully. Developer 4A Games’ (read our new interview with them about how Russia's invasion of Ukraine changed their development approach) proprietary engine is really cooking here, though I should confess that framerate isn’t something I can reasonably report on right now – not just because I was playing a preview build of a game that won’t be out for six months, but also because I was playing it remotely via GeForce Now. So we’ll have to see how it holds up once I can throw my own 5080 at it, rather than the 5080 that was feeding the game to me via the cloud.

I’ve come this far in this preview and I still feel like I’ve barely scratched the surface of what Metro 2039 is offering. Series veterans have no dou bt already been nodding their heads along in satisfaction, while those new to Metro are in for a treat – if the few hours I got to play are any indication. February 2027 was already looking stacked with the first big wave of post-GTA 6 releases, but Metro 2039 just cemented itself on my must-play list for that crowded month.

articles.title: Metro 2039 Developers on How Russia's Invasion of Ukraine Changed Their Plans
articles.summary: After finishing the four-or-so-hour preview build of Metro 2039, the upcoming first-person shooter sequel from Ukrainian developer 4A Games and falling completely in love with it, I reached out to the team to ask some questions about how they've approached the latest entry in their post-apocalyptic franchise – both in terms of the game itself, but also because their real lives have changed so much since Russia's invasion of their country in 2022.
articles.body:
After finishing the four-or-so-hour preview build of Metro 2039, the upcoming first-person shooter sequel from Ukrainian developer 4A Games and falling completely in love with it , I reached out to the team to ask some questions about how they've approached the latest entry in their post-apocalyptic franchise – both in terms of the game itself, but also in terms of how their real lives have changed since Russia's invasion of their country in 2022.

"First of all, it's impacted the team," said creative director Andriy "MLS" Shevchenko. "The world changes the team completely, their way of being, their way of thinking, and their way of understanding what's going on in general. So automatically it brings new visions and new philosophy into the game through the team. And everything else is just details. Story changed? Yes. Some gameplay elements changed? Yes. But first of all, it's the team."

"And I would say that effect on the team did actually directly affect the story in the way that previous Metro games were about the prevention of war," said executive producer Jon Bloch. "And when Russia started its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it brought war to our doorsteps and we had to change our approach about what kind of story we wanted to tell. We wanted to tell now the consequences of war, what happens when war comes to you. And so it was a pretty major change to what we were doing. We had to try to see from a production standpoint what we could save and what needed to change. We tried to save as much as we could, but quite a lot of our plans changed overnight."

"Yeah, that's true," added co-creative director and audio lead Pavel Ulmer. "And the very Metro franchise, its very nature just became too close to reality. So the perception changed dramatically. Basically, it's all divided from before and after."

Pivoting to the game itself, I asked what lessons they've taken from previous Metro games and applied to 2039. "Avoid empty spaces," Shevchenko said. "The density of everything, it's our goal and the thing to be proud of now." Bloch added: "To that last question, to that last answer, density is a big one. Density of objects, density of sound, density of animation, density of characters, density of everything, density of detail. We rebuilt our render from the ground up to be fully ray traced and really push forward on the realistic picture that we can provide and the amount of assets that we can put into the world, the amount of dynamic things that we can put into the world, and all of that while still retaining performance and running on all platforms. The engine from day one has always been multi-platform. So performance is a huge, huge factor for us. But a lot of the things that we did were with the goal of increasing the amount of stuff that we can do, giving our designers and our artists more freedom, taking away a lot of the barriers that they have to be able to do what they want while still retaining performance."

"So basically our goal is not to make the area cool only where the cut scene is supposed to be, you know, but to make all the areas look cool and nice and natural, believable," Ulmer noted.

Finally, I asked the Metro team what tips they'd give to new players for whom Metro 2039 will be their first game in the series. "Do not be afraid to explore," Shevchenko suggested. "Explore and you will find a lot of interesting things." Ulmer added, "Do not rush," before Bloch chimed in: "Metro is a slow burn. It's not fast-paced. We have fast-paced action sequences, but overall, it's something you sit and absorb. You spend the time to learn about the story, the atmosphere, everything. And it's something for people who want to observe and to think, to question things. It's something we hope is more meaningful."

"For our younger audience, I might say, use sprint only when you really have to," Ulmer suggested. "Don't sprint through the game all over the place. There's a lot of things to enjoy, as Jon mentioned, a lot of things to hear, to think about, just to absorb the atmosphere. So sprint only when you actually have to sprint, running from a lot of threats that will try to chase you. In that case, go for it. But it's like a good movie. Playing this story just in order to finish, it's a bad idea. Enjoy it. Take your time."
